q: On which date did the Reserve Bank of India start its operations?
explain: The RBI Act was passed in 1934, but operations began on 1 April 1935. 1 January 1949 is the date of nationalisation.

q: Which commission’s 1926 report recommended the creation of a central bank for India?
explain: The Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance, popularly the Hilton Young Commission, recommended a central bank in 1926.

q: The head office of the RBI was permanently moved from Calcutta to Mumbai in:
explain: RBI began in Calcutta (Kolkata) and shifted permanently to Mumbai in 1937.

q: When was the Reserve Bank of India nationalised?
explain: The Reserve Bank (Transfer of Public Ownership) Act, 1948 took effect on 1 January 1949, making RBI government-owned.

q: Under which Act was the RBI taken over from its private shareholders?
options: Reserve Bank (Transfer of Public Ownership) Act, 1948
Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970
explain: The 1948 Transfer of Public Ownership Act nationalised RBI with compensation to shareholders. The 1970 Act relates to commercial banks.

q: What was the RBI’s opening share capital?
explain: RBI started with ₹5 crore divided into fully paid shares of ₹100 each, mostly held by private shareholders.

q: Who was the first Governor of the RBI, serving from 1 April 1935 to 30 June 1937?
explain: Sir Osborne Smith was the first Governor; James Braid Taylor succeeded him in July 1937.

q: Who was the first Indian to become Governor of the RBI?
explain: C. D. Deshmukh took over on 11 August 1943 and was the first Indian Governor. Taylor, the second Governor, was British.

q: From 2020-21 onwards, which period does the RBI’s accounting year cover?
explain: RBI earlier followed July to June but moved to the April to March year from 2020-21, in line with banks and the government.

q: As per the syllabus, how many members does the RBI’s Central Board of Directors have?
explain: The board has 20 members: Governor (1), Deputy Governors (4), Directors (4), Executive Directors (10) and a government official (1).

q: The Central Board of Directors of the RBI is appointed or nominated for a period of how many years?
explain: The board is appointed or nominated by the Government of India for four years.

q: Which of the following is NOT a fully owned subsidiary of the RBI?
options: Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation
Reserve Bank Information Technology Private Limited
Indian Financial Technology and Allied Services
Small Industries Development Bank of India
explain: RBI’s fully owned subsidiaries are DICGC, BRBNMPL, ReBIT and IFTAS. SIDBI is a separate development financial institution.

q: Which RBI subsidiary is responsible for printing Indian currency notes?
options: Bharatiya Reserve Bank Note Mudran Private Limited
Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation
Reserve Bank Information Technology Private Limited
explain: BRBNMPL prints notes. DICGC insures deposits and ReBIT handles IT; NPCI is a separate payments organisation.

q: Which of the following is NOT a function of the Reserve Bank of India?
options: Acting as banker to the government
Accepting deposits from the general public
explain: RBI does not take deposits from, or lend to, the general public; it deals with the government and banks.

q: A bank that acts as the banker of other banks is called a:
explain: The central bank (RBI in India) keeps the accounts of scheduled banks and is the bankers’ bank.

q: Which currency is issued by the Government of India rather than by the RBI?
explain: One rupee notes and all coins are issued by the Government of India, while other notes are issued by the RBI.

q: Under which section of the RBI Act does the Reserve Bank have the sole right to issue bank notes?
explain: Section 22 gives RBI the sole right of note issue. Section 20 covers central government business and Section 21A state government business.

q: Consider these roles: I. currency authority, II. controlling money supply and credit, III. managing foreign exchange, IV. banker to the government. Which are functions of the RBI?
options: All four: I, II, III and IV
explain: RBI performs all four roles, along with regulation of banks, banking for banks and a developmental role.

q: Which animal appears in the emblem of the RBI?
explain: The RBI emblem shows a tiger standing beneath a palm tree.

q: The methods of credit control used by the RBI can be broadly divided into:
explain: Quantitative (general) tools control the overall volume of credit; qualitative (selective) tools direct credit to specific uses.

q: Which of the following is a qualitative tool of credit control?
explain: Moral suasion is a selective, informal tool. Bank rate, CRR and OMO are quantitative.

q: Which of the following is NOT a quantitative measure of monetary policy?
explain: Margin requirements are a qualitative tool. SLR, bank rate and OMO are quantitative.

q: What is the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)?
options: Share of deposits banks must invest in government securities
Rate at which banks borrow from the RBI
Rate at which the RBI borrows from banks
Share of deposits banks must keep as cash with the RBI
explain: CRR is the percentage of a bank’s deposits kept as cash with the RBI. The first option describes SLR.

q: Which statement about the Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) is correct?
options: Banks keep it as cash with the RBI
It is the rate at which the RBI lends to banks
Banks hold it themselves in cash, gold or approved securities
It must be held only in the form of gold
explain: SLR is held by the bank itself as liquid assets: cash, gold and unencumbered approved securities. CRR is the one kept with the RBI.

q: Reverse repo is a tool used by the RBI to:
options: Absorb liquidity from the banking system
Inject liquidity into the banking system
Fix the base rate of banks
explain: In reverse repo the RBI borrows from banks, which soaks up surplus liquidity.

q: The rate at which the central bank lends short-term funds to commercial banks is called:
explain: Repo is the short-term rate at which the RBI lends against securities. Reverse repo is the rate at which it borrows.

q: To curb excess liquidity in the economy, the RBI can:
explain: A higher CRR leaves banks with less to lend and cuts money supply. The other options add liquidity.

q: Open market operations (OMO) mean:
options: Auction of gold by the RBI
Issue of different kinds of bonds by banks
Sale and purchase of government securities by the RBI
explain: OMO is the RBI’s buying and selling of government securities to manage money supply: buying injects funds, selling absorbs them.

q: The Statutory Liquidity Ratio is the ratio of liquid assets to a bank’s:
explain: SLR is expressed as a percentage of net demand and time liabilities (NDTL), as is CRR.

q: The bank rate is best described as:
options: The interest rate on savings deposits
The rate at which the RBI re-discounts bills of exchange and approved securities of banks
The rate at which banks lend to their best customers
The rate at which the RBI borrows from banks
explain: The bank rate is the RBI’s re-discounting rate. It now follows the repo rate, which guides banks’ own rates.

q: As per the figures in the 2024-25 syllabus, the CRR and SLR stand at:
explain: The snapshot lists CRR at 4.50% and SLR at 18%, with repo at 6.50%. These rates change at policy reviews.

q: Moral suasion refers to:
options: A penal interest rate on excess credit
Informal, psychological persuasion of banks by the RBI
Refusal to rediscount bills of banks
Fixing minimum down payments on consumer loans
explain: Moral suasion works through requests and persuasion. The other options describe direct action and consumer credit regulation.

q: The RBI refuses to rediscount the papers of a bank that fails its requirements, or charges it a penal rate. This tool is called:
explain: Direct action is the penalising step taken against banks that do not meet conditions set by the RBI.

q: A margin requirement refers to the:
options: Gap between the value of the security offered and the amount borrowed
Share of deposits kept as cash with the RBI
Rate at which the RBI lends to banks
Limit on the number of branches a bank can open
explain: The margin is the difference between the security’s value and the loan given, and it is a qualitative tool.

q: The Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) was introduced for the first time in:
explain: LAF began in June 2000 to help banks manage day-to-day liquidity mismatches through repo and reverse repo.

q: The Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) came into effect on:
explain: MSF was announced in the 2011-12 policy and took effect on 9 May 2014. 25 August 2011 is when the Nair Committee on PSL was set up.

q: From April 2016, MCLR replaced which system of fixing lending rates?
explain: The Base Rate system, introduced in July 2010, was replaced by the Marginal Cost of funds based Lending Rate from April 2016.

q: In August 2011 the RBI set up a committee under which person to re-examine the classification of priority sector lending?
explain: The M. V. Nair Committee, set up on 25 August 2011, reviewed priority sector classification and suggested revised guidelines.

q: How many members does the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) have?
explain: The MPC has six members: three RBI officials and three external members nominated by the government.

q: The MPC’s inflation target is 4%. What is the tolerance band around it?
explain: The mandate is 4% inflation with a lower tolerance of 2% and an upper tolerance of 6%.

q: Which of the following was NOT a member of the Monetary Policy Committee in 2018?
explain: The Finance Minister is not on the MPC. The Governor, Deputy Governor Acharya and executive director Patra were RBI-side members.

q: The Monetary Policy Committee is constituted under which section of the RBI Act, 1934?
explain: Section 45ZB provides for the MPC. Section 22 is note issue and Section 20 is central government business.

q: RBI carries out the receipts and payments of the Central Government under which section of the RBI Act, 1934?
explain: Section 20 obliges RBI to handle the Centre’s receipts, payments and public debt. State business falls under Section 21A.

q: As per the syllabus, RBI has agreements for conducting state government business with all states except:
explain: Under Section 21A agreements exist with every state government except Sikkim, as per the syllabus.

q: On which date did the RBI Central Board meet to consider the government’s advice to withdraw ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes?
explain: The government advised on 7 November 2016 and the board met the very next day, 8 November.

q: According to the RBI, what share of the demonetised notes had returned to the banking system?
explain: About ₹15.31 lakh crore out of ₹15.41 lakh crore, or 99.3%, came back.

q: Who was the RBI Governor from 4 September 2013 to 4 September 2016?
explain: Raghuram Rajan served between Subbarao (2008-13) and Urjit Patel (2016-18).

q: Who took over as RBI Governor from Urjit Patel in December 2018?
explain: Shaktikanta Das became the 25th Governor on 11 December 2018.

q: Which future Prime Minister served as RBI Governor from 1982 to 1985?
explain: Manmohan Singh was Governor from 16 September 1982 to 14 January 1985. Rangarajan and Jalan came later and were never Prime Minister.

q: Who had the shortest tenure as RBI Governor, from 15 January to 4 February 1985?
explain: Amitav Ghosh served only about three weeks. Adarkar and Ambegaonkar served around six weeks, Sen Gupta three months.

q: Which of the following Acts is NOT administered by the RBI?
explain: The Competition Act is only a relevant Act. RBI administers FEMA, the Banking Regulation Act and the Payment and Settlement Systems Act.

q: Who headed the RBI committee on a Public Credit Registry for India?
explain: The High Level Task Force on Public Credit Registry (June 2018) was headed by Y. M. Deosthalee.

q: The RBI committee on deepening of digital payments (2019) was headed by:
explain: Nandan Nilekani headed the May 2019 committee on deepening digital payments. U. K. Sinha headed the MSME committee.

q: What is the full form of CIC, for which RBI set up a committee to strengthen corporate governance?
explain: CIC stands for Core Investment Company. RBI had a Working Group on Core Investment Companies headed by Tapan Ray.

q: Which three-year roadmap finalised by the RBI aims to improve regulation and supervision, among other functions?
explain: Utkarsh 2022 was the RBI’s medium-term strategy framework; Utkarsh 2.0 later covered 2023-2025.

q: The RBI’s UDGAM portal helps the public to locate their:
options: Fixed deposits in a single bank
explain: UDGAM stands for Unclaimed Deposits – Gateway to Access inforMation, a central portal for tracing unclaimed deposits.

q: After how many years without operation are savings or current account balances classified as unclaimed deposits and moved to the DEA Fund?
explain: Balances not operated for 10 years, or term deposits not claimed within 10 years of maturity, go to the Depositor Education and Awareness Fund.

q: Which dashboard did the RBI launch to monitor the progress of financial inclusion?
explain: Antardrishti is the financial inclusion dashboard launched by the RBI Governor.

q: For how many years were Floating Rate Savings Bonds 2020 (Taxable), offered on the RBI Retail Direct portal, issued?
explain: FRSB 2020 (T) are seven-year bonds available to retail investors through RBI Retail Direct.

q: Which parameter carries the highest weight in the RBI Digital Payments Index (RBI-DPI)?
explain: The weights are Payment Enablers 25%, demand-side 10%, supply-side 15%, Payment Performance 45% and Consumer Centricity 5%.
